title: A person starts their own lifemodel instance from the Docker image with one command
description:
Charter: docs/charters/instance-1.md, outcome 4 (re-cut 2026-10-08). Design decisions (1)-(16) with their evidence are in this issue's comments; this body is the spec.

## Problem
Today lifemodel runs only from a developer's checkout: `npm run dev` with an `.env`, Node and native libraries installed by hand, keys in plain environment variables the agent's own process can read, nothing that stops it or brings it back when it breaks. A person who wants their own lifemodel cannot start one, and an agent that rewrites its own code holds every key and can disable anything meant to stop it.

## Solution
A person runs one `docker run` command with the published image. They open `boot.localhost` (through an SSH tunnel on a VPS), set the loader's password, and the loader brings up lifemodel. They put the model key into Agent Vault (`vault.localhost`, reached through the loader's login), open lifemodel's own interface at the root host and set the endpoint and the models. lifemodel then talks to the model with the key injected on the way out, never holding it. The owner can panic the instance from the loader or the command line, and it stays down through restarts until resumed. Recreating the container keeps lifemodel's code and data.

## Stories
- S1 First start. As a person with Docker, I run the documented command on an empty volume; the loader starts, `boot.localhost` asks me to set a password, and after I set it the loader creates the instance's git repository on the volume from the code the image carries, builds it, and starts lifemodel. Nothing asks me for a key at this point.
- S2 Login. Every page of `boot.`, the root host and `vault.` requires the loader's login; one login (a cookie on the parent domain) opens all three; a wrong password is refused and logged at warn without the password.
- S3 Keys. As the owner I add the model key to Agent Vault through `vault.` (its own interface) and a service for my endpoint's host with bearer auth. lifemodel's settings show only a placeholder and a link to the loader for keys. The key never appears in lifemodel's process environment, its config, its logs or its data.
- S4 lifemodel's settings. In lifemodel's own interface at the root host I set the OpenAI-compatible endpoint (base URL), the model for each role (fast, smart, motor), and the Telegram fields (chat id; the bot token as an Agent Vault placeholder). Saving applies them: lifemodel restarts through the loader with the new settings. These settings belong to lifemodel's code, which may extend them later.
- S5 A model request. lifemodel's request to the endpoint leaves through Agent Vault; the endpoint receives `Authorization: Bearer <the key from Agent Vault>`. A direct connection from lifemodel's user that bypasses the proxy is refused by the kernel rule, and that refusal is visible in lifemodel's log as a connection error, not a silent hang.
- S6 Panic. `docker exec <c> lifemodel panic` or the loader's button stops lifemodel (its turn drained as on any stop) and marks panic in a place lifemodel's user cannot write. While panic is set, the loader stays up but does not start lifemodel - after `docker restart` and after a restart of the Docker daemon alike. `lifemodel resume` (or the button) clears it and starts lifemodel. `lifemodel status` says whether lifemodel runs, on which commit, and whether panic is set.
- S7 Recreate. `docker rm -f` and the same `docker run` on the same volume bring back the same instance: the same repository and commit, the same data, the same loader password and Agent Vault contents; the image's code does not overwrite the instance's repository.
- S8 Stop. `docker stop` gives lifemodel its drain (the restart guarantee of outcome 2) before the container ends; the documented command sets a stop timeout long enough for it.
- S9 Image. Every pull request that touches product code builds the image in CI as a check; every push to main publishes it to `ghcr.io/shady2k/lifemodel` (tags `main` and the commit).

## Decisions
- The image holds the runtime (Node 24, native libraries for onnx, sharp, LanceDB, git) and a TRUSTED LAYER lifemodel cannot see or change: the LOADER, CADDY and AGENT VAULT, run as root-owned processes; lifemodel runs as an unprivileged user. The loader starts first and owns the others; it is the container's main process.
- Volume layout (one volume): the instance's git repository (lifemodel's code; seeded once from the code the image carries, with upstream as a remote; never overwritten by a newer image), the build of the current commit, lifemodel's data (state, logs, config, models), and root-only directories for the loader (password hash, panic flag, its own state) and Agent Vault (its store, passwordless mode: protection is the directory's permissions).
- Only what lifemodel must not change sits in the loader: its login, panic, first start. Model endpoint, models, Telegram and every other setting are lifemodel's own (decision 9). Generations, self-healing and maintenance are outcome 5.
- The loader's web interface is always on, independent of lifemodel. Its command line inside the container is `lifemodel status|panic|resume`.
- Front door: Caddy is the only web entrance. Routing by host: the root host is lifemodel's interface, `boot.` the loader, `vault.` Agent Vault (its interface uses absolute paths, so it cannot sit under a subpath). Caddy asks the loader to check every request (forward_auth); one cookie on the parent domain. Listens on localhost only in this outcome; built so a domain and certificates can be added later (idea lifemodel-sd2).
- lifemodel's egress: an iptables owner rule lets lifemodel's user connect only to Agent Vault's proxy port (and loopback services it needs); the rule is installed by the loader as root before lifemodel starts; the container needs NET_ADMIN, and nothing else beyond defaults. lifemodel's vault in Agent Vault is NOT strict: known services get their key, other hosts pass through (lifemodel reads news and the web); strict deny is for tasks (outcome 6). lifemodel's process uses the proxy through the standard proxy environment and trusts Agent Vault's CA.
- Keys: the model key by bearer auth on the endpoint's host; the Telegram token by placeholder substitution in the request path (Agent Vault supports path, query, header and body substitution). lifemodel's config holds placeholders only.
- lifemodel's model configuration becomes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint (base URL) with a model per role; no key in lifemodel. The existing provider code is extended, not duplicated (one surface per capability); OpenRouter remains reachable as just another OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
- Agent Vault's version is pinned in the image and updated deliberately (its API is still changing).
- Embeddings stay local (downloaded to the volume on first use).
- Failures explain themselves: the loader logs to stdout (the container log) with a component name; a refused login, a failed first build, a refused start under panic and a stop that ran past the drain are each one line saying what and why; secrets never appear in any log.

## Checks
The seams, all reached from outside the container the way a person does:
- C1 the documented `docker run` command and `docker exec <c> lifemodel status|panic|resume` (exit codes and output);
- C2 HTTP against Caddy with `Host:` headers `boot.localhost`, `localhost`, `vault.localhost` (login refused/accepted, pages reachable only with the cookie);
- C3 a STUB OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the test environment that answers a fixed completion and records the headers it receives: proves the key arrives injected;
- C4 lifemodel's process environment, config file and logs inside the container contain no key (checked by reading them);
- C5 a direct connection from lifemodel's user to an outside address is refused;
- C6 `docker restart`, a restart of the Docker daemon, `docker rm -f` + `docker run` on the same volume;
- C7 the CI workflow: the image builds on a pull request with product changes and is published on main.
Unit tests through the loader's own interfaces (first start, panic flag, login) with doubles only at the process and filesystem boundaries; the end-to-end walk above is the acceptance. The model key used is a made-up string; no real Telegram or keys.

## Out
- Generations, self-healing, maintenance mode, migrations (outcome 5).
- The task executor and Motor Cortex without Docker (outcome 6); in the image Motor Cortex answers that Docker is unavailable, as it already does.
- Access from outside: own domain, certificates, Let's Encrypt (idea lifemodel-sd2).
- Remote embeddings; custom request headers (lifemodel adds them later itself).
- Spend limits (lifemodel-ld6).
- Updates from upstream into an existing instance (upstream-1).

## DONE WHEN
On a clean test machine with Docker, one command starts the image from CI; the owner sets the loader's password, puts the model key into Agent Vault through the loader, sets the endpoint and models in lifemodel's own interface; lifemodel's model request reaches the endpoint with the key injected by Agent Vault while no key is in lifemodel's process; recreating the container keeps the code and the data; panic keeps it down across a restart of the container and of Docker until it is resumed. Where it is seen: the browser at boot.localhost / localhost / vault.localhost (through an SSH tunnel on a VPS), `docker exec <c> lifemodel status`, and the stub endpoint's recorded request.

Docs current/present gategreen; eight old path reports are documented runtime artifacts, not new repo dead links. Privacyiie/JSON2g2 remain deferred. No owner-host walk or real public Telegram claimed; closure records publish via land workflow.

comments.author: claude-coordinator:shady2k@vm-agents:main#e5607568
comments.text:
Owner decisions 2026-10-08 (design discussion for instance-1 outcomes 4-6; research by two background reads, key claims checked):
(1) Motor Cortex becomes a TASK EXECUTOR: several tasks at once, one prime-agent per task, each with its own profile (files, network, resources, time); self-change is one kind of task, others work on other repositories. prime-agent is lifemodel's hands: a self-change task has full access to the instance's code and data. lifemodel picks a task's profile, the owner sets the ceilings; a trusted executor baked into the image (root, beside the supervisor) launches and confines each task and refuses a request above the ceilings.
(2) Isolation inside the one container (only Docker on the host): per-task uid + Landlock (files) + an iptables owner rule sending the task's traffic only to the egress proxy + rlimits. Evidence: in a default Docker container user/net namespaces are blocked (unshare -U: Operation not permitted, tested here), so srt/Codex sandbox/bubblewrap/nsjail/firejail/gVisor do not fit; Landlock ABI 7 works (tested); /sys/fs/cgroup is read-only (no per-task cgroups; container-wide --memory/--cpus is the outer cap). Needs one container capability: NET_ADMIN. Ready-made per-task platforms either need KVM (microsandbox, E2B, Docker Sandboxes, Kata, Firecracker) or host-root via the Docker socket / privileged DinD (Daytona OSS, container-use, OpenHands) - rejected.
(3) The executor's interface is shaped so microsandbox (microVM per task, host-side domain policy, TS SDK, only --device /dev/kvm) can be added later as a second backend where KVM exists.
(4) Secrets never enter task processes (and, where feasible, not lifemodel itself): all task egress goes through Infisical Agent Vault (github.com/Infisical/agent-vault, MIT core) in strict-deny mode - it is the domain allowlist and injects credentials from placeholders; per-task role = allowed services + credentials. Its management port is unreachable to tasks (iptables allows only the proxy port); tasks trust its MITM CA (NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS). OpenBao dropped: Agent Vault's own encrypted store suffices; Infisical as a source later for short-lived secrets. Owner uses Agent Vault in his homelab.

comments.author: claude-coordinator:shady2k@vm-agents:main#e5607568
comments.text:
Owner decisions 2026-10-08, continued:
(5) Name: the trusted component is the LOADER (the project's word from ADR-006: a trusted loader runs numbered generations, boot-state, A/B slots for its own update); 'supervisor' is not used. The loader is also the BOOTSTRAP: an empty volume opens the setup wizard (model endpoint and key, models, Telegram, embeddings local or remote); every later start boots the selected generation. One entry point for install, normal boot and maintenance.
(6) Maintenance mode 'like BIOS/UEFI': the loader lists generations and the owner picks one to boot; entered by hand (a start flag or docker exec) or automatically after N consecutive generations fail to come up. Self-healing: a new generation that does not come up healthy is replaced by the previous healthy one, with a report.
(7) The loader has its OWN WEB INTERFACE (not Telegram) for the setup wizard, the generation list and panic: by default it listens on localhost only (access through an SSH tunnel); the owner may open it outside behind his own HTTPS proxy.
(8) DATA IS NEVER ROLLED BACK - a generation is code only; Telegram history and external memory cannot be rolled back anyway. Compatibility: data format changes are expanding by preference; a breaking change ships an up/down migration pair with a format version; when switching back the loader runs the down migration taken from the generation being left (still on disk) before starting the older one; a failed down leaves data untouched and refuses the switch with a report; a generation that sees a newer format with no way back does not start silently. The self-change gates check a migration pair round-trip (up then down restores the data) and refuse a breaking change without it. Builds on the plugin loader's lifecycle.migrate/hotSwap (ADR-006).

comments.author: claude-coordinator:shady2k@vm-agents:main#e5607568
comments.text:
Owner decisions 2026-10-08, continued (supersedes the wizard contents of (5)):
(9) What belongs to the loader: ONLY what lifemodel must not be able to change itself - access to the loader interface, panic, generations (list, boot, maintenance, self-healing), the files/resources/concurrency ceilings of tasks, first start (seed the instance repository, build and start generation 1). Everything else - model endpoint, models per role, request headers (precedent: in ouroboros the owner asked the agent to add custom headers and it did), Telegram, embeddings (a change is lifemodel's own migration), personality, timezone, web search - is lifemodel's OWN settings in its OWN web interface, which it can extend itself. The loader is the way out when lifemodel has become a brick.
(10) The loader's setup asks only for its password; first acquaintance and settings are led by lifemodel's own interface.
(11) The loader's web interface runs ALWAYS, beside lifemodel, independent of it; changes made there apply immediately (panic at once; a changed key from the next request; network rules even for running tasks; files/resources only for new tasks - Landlock and rlimits cannot change on a running process; the loader may offer to stop a running task).
(12) Keys, network and access of tasks are managed in Agent Vault's OWN management interface, served through the loader's web server (e.g. /vault): one address, its port never published and unreachable to tasks. lifemodel sees placeholders only; keys are injected per request. Task ceilings split: network + keys = an Agent Vault role; files, resources, concurrency = the loader. Agent Vault's version is pinned in the image (its API is still changing). Trusted layer = loader + task executor + Agent Vault; lifemodel and tasks can neither see nor change it.

comments.author: claude-coordinator:shady2k@vm-agents:main#e5607568
comments.text: Owner decisions 2026-10-08, preflight of outcome 4: (13) the front door is CADDY (not nginx): the only web entrance, routing by subdomain - boot. the loader, app. lifemodel's own interface, vault. Agent Vault (its UI uses absolute /v1 paths, 37 places, so it cannot live under a subpath) - each app at the root of its host; one login by a cookie on the parent domain, checked by the loader through forward_auth; local only by default (*.localhost through an SSH tunnel). Built so a domain and certificates can be added without rework. (14) Access from outside (own domain, own certificate or Let's Encrypt) is LATER, kept as an idea (lifemodel-sd2).

The endpoint in the test environment is a stub OpenAI-compatible server that records the headers it receives; the key is a made-up string. title: The loader starts lifemodel from the instance's repository on the volume, holds panic and one login
description:
Stage lifemodel-q4x.2, spec stories S1, S2, S6, S7, S8 (feature lifemodel-q4x body).
The loader: a TypeScript program in its own directory of the repository (not under src/, which is the instance's code), compiled into the image, run as the container's main process (root). It: on an empty volume serves boot.localhost's password page; after the password: seeds the instance's git repository on the volume from the code the image carries (upstream as a remote), builds it (npm ci, npm run build), starts lifemodel (node dist/index.js) as an unprivileged user with DATA_PATH on the volume; forwards SIGTERM and waits for lifemodel's drain; restarts lifemodel when it dies (backoff); keeps panic in a root-only flag (panic stops lifemodel and blocks its start until resume); answers forward_auth for every host (cookie on the parent domain; wrong password refused, logged at warn without the password); CLI lifemodel status|panic|resume; on an existing volume never re-seeds; its own state (password hash, panic) root-only on the volume.
Criterion: tests through the loader's interfaces with doubles only at process/filesystem boundaries show: first start seeds and starts once, a second start reuses the repository; panic set -> start refused (and normally starts); resume clears; wrong password refused (right one accepted, cookie valid for boot., root, vault. hosts); SIGTERM waits for the child's exit.

title: The signal-forwarding test leaves no stand-in Caddy or Agent Vault process running, however it ends
description:
What a person does: runs the suite (or tests/integration/loader-signal-forwarding.test.ts), and the run is interrupted, times out or a test fails.
What happens: the stand-in Caddy (/tmp/loader-signal-*/caddy run ...) and Agent Vault (node /tmp/loader-signal-*/agent-vault server ...) processes the test starts keep running, re-parented to init. On 2026-10-09, 11 were found alive on the shared machine, the oldest 16 h, each holding CPU, memory and loopback ports.
What should happen: when the test file ends in any way - pass, fail, timeout, the vitest process interrupted - none of the processes it started is left running.

Out: the temp directories themselves (the sibling finding about loader tests' temp dirs).

title: The loader tests remove every temporary directory they create

title: Agent Vault runs in the image under the loader, reached at vault. behind the one login, its store root-only
description:

Criterion: in the image, after first start, vault.localhost with the login shows Agent Vault's UI (and 401 without it); its store directory is root 0700; a second start reuses the store (and normally creates it on an empty volume); a gated Docker test proves it.

comments.text:
submitted: feature/lifemodel-q4x-vault@f53d7be -- Agent Vault runs in the image under the loader, behind vault. and the one login, its store root-only

Three commits: 753e517 (the loader module, config, wiring, unit tests), 97c6ad0
(the pinned binary in the image, the gated container walk, the documents),
f53d7be (the stop-during-start guards).

What it does: the loader starts Agent Vault 0.40.0 (release binary, checked
against the release's checksums.txt at build time, amd64 and arm64) before
lifemodel, keeps it up with the same growing backoff as Caddy, and stops it
after lifemodel inside the stop's one deadline. Its store is passwordless
(`server --password-stdin` with an empty line, decision 4) at
/var/lib/lifemodel/vault (root 0700, its HOME); its API is 127.0.0.1:14321 and
its proxy 127.0.0.1:14322; its CA is exported to /var/lib/lifemodel/vault-ca.pem
(root 0644, readable by uid 1000 and not writable). The loader registers the
instance owner account (owner@lifemodel.local, generated password, root-only
loader/vault-owner.json), creates the vault `lifemodel` and the agent
`lifemodel` with the vault role proxy, keeps the token root-only in
loader/vault-proxy.json, and gives lifemodel's process AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN/ADDR/
VAULT and nothing else (loader/src/agent-vault.ts:lifemodelEnvironment is the
one place lifemodel-q4x.3.2 adds the proxy variables). Idempotent: a second
start re-reads the record and re-reads only the CA; a lost token is rotated
rather than a second agent created. A missing binary, a store it cannot
prepare, a server that does not answer within 15 s (or exits first) and a
failed provisioning are each one line with the cause and a non-zero exit.

Checks: `npm run check` exit 0 (139 files, 2370 tests passed, 17 skipped,
23.7 s). Gated container walk: LIFEMODEL_DOCKER_TESTS=1 npx vitest run
--maxWorkers=2 tests/integration/instance-first-start.test.ts -> 8 passed in
132.1 s (the store/CA/listeners test 597 ms, the restart-reuses-the-store test
1445 ms). `npm run backlog` green, `npm run present` 0 new errors. Every rule
has a test that fails without it: removing the passwordless stdin line, the CA
mode, the store-mode repair, the token in lifemodel's environment, the
provisioning call, the stale-pid-file removal, the token reuse, the Agent Vault
stop in the shutdown, and each of the three stop-during-start guards fails its
test (13 removals tried, 13 caught).

Decided alone: (1) the loader registers the instance owner account in Agent
Vault with generated credentials it keeps root-only - the task asks the loader
to create the vault and the agent token idempotently, and Agent Vault gives no
unauthenticated way to do that; how the human owner reaches that account in the
vault UI is not solved here (named as a doubt in the worker report, and a
candidate for the acceptance walk lifemodel-q4x.1). (2) the store is
passwordless by construction: AGENT_VAULT_MASTER_PASSWORD and AGENT_VAULT_ADDR
are dropped from the child's environment and telemetry is off. (3) a pid file
left in the store is removed before a start (Agent Vault refuses a start when
that pid belongs to a live process, and a killed server leaves the file).

title: lifemodel serves its own settings interface at the root host: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a model per role, Telegram; saving restarts it through the loader
description:
Stage lifemodel-q4x.4 (spec S4; decisions 9, 10, 15). lifemodel (src/, the instance's evolving code) serves a small web interface on 127.0.0.1:7100 (behind Caddy and the loader's login; no auth of its own): the OpenAI-compatible endpoint base URL, the model for fast/smart/motor, the Telegram chat id and the bot token as an Agent Vault placeholder (e.g. __telegram_bot_token__), a link to the loader (boot.) for keys. Settings persist in lifemodel's config on the volume (data/config/agent.json through the existing config path) and apply by a restart: lifemodel asks the loader to restart it (a narrow loader endpoint lifemodel may call: restart only, nothing else - panic, keys and ceilings stay out of its reach) or exits with a code the loader restarts on. The model configuration becomes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint with per-role models and no key, extending the existing provider code (createLLMProvider / the local provider path) instead of adding a parallel one; OpenRouter keeps working as one more OpenAI-compatible endpoint. title: Tests that run git never touch the repository whose hook started them
description:
A repair the merge of stage lifemodel-q4x.4 waits on (not a finding).

What a person does: commits in this repository with the husky pre-commit hook active (`npm ci` re-enables it through `prepare: husky`; its .husky/pre-commit runs `npx vitest run`).
What happens: git runs the hook with GIT_DIR, GIT_INDEX_FILE (and on a worktree GIT_WORK_TREE/GIT_COMMON_DIR) set; the suite inherits them, and every test that runs git in a temporary directory (loader-seed-git, ci-product-paths, build-image, instance-*, container-image, tool-server-utils, and the loader code they drive) acts on the REAL repository instead. On 2026-10-09 the merge commit of feature/lifemodel-q4x-settings into feature/lifemodel-q4x-instance got a fixture's tree, 14 fixture commits landed on the feature branch, and .git/config was rewritten (bare=true, origin renamed to upstream, core.hooksPath to a deleted temp dir, a test user, gpgsign off, a branch upstream). The owner restored the config by hand; the branch is restored from its reflog (364761a).
What should happen: no test can reach any repository but its own temporary one, wherever the suite is started from (a hook, a shell, CI).

DONE WHEN: (1) the vitest setup removes every GIT_* variable from the environment before any test runs; (2) a guard test runs a git fixture with GIT_DIR/GIT_INDEX_FILE pointing at a sentinel repository and shows the sentinel untouched (and turns red when the scrub is removed); (3) .husky/pre-commit unsets GIT_* before it runs tests; (4) a real `git commit` with the husky hook active in a scratch clone leaves that clone's history and config unchanged apart from the commit itself.
Out: changing which hook a clone uses (`npm run connect` owns that).

title: A disposable launcher bounds and isolates ordinary and Docker test runs
description:
## Problem
Tests started from hooks or shells can alter the real repository, load the owner environment, leave processes and temporary data behind, and overload the machine. Existing fixes on the instance branch do not provide a launch-level boundary.
## Solution
Run local checks and tests through one disposable isolated launcher, also used by CI and hooks. Ordinary tests receive a private source snapshot and disposable HOME/TMP/data with Node 24 and lockfile dependencies, no owner git metadata, secrets, state, or Docker socket. Docker integration tests get a separate disposable daemon, not the owner daemon. Limit CPU, memory, pids, concurrent launches and total runtime. Preserve test exit status and reports. Cleanup from outside the test process on success, failure, timeout and interruption.
## Decisions
Owner 2026-10-09: tests must run locally, but isolated; approved implementation ('Делай'). Workers use shady2k-gateway/glm-5.3-flash. This is a repair of the instance acceptance launch, not a new milestone outcome. Build from main without bundling the unfinished instance product. Never run the existing suite directly on the host. No daemon socket mount or privileged test process. If nested daemon implementation needs a weaker host boundary, stop and report rather than silently grant it.
## Checks
One CLI runs ordinary check/test commands and Docker integration mode. An isolated sentinel scenario proves hostile GIT_* and owner environment/files absent, fixture git cannot mutate the source checkout, and interruption/timeout removes processes and test resources. Static tests cover launch policy and failure paths; real Docker acceptance checks successful test, failing test, cancellation and timeout. Full check runs only through isolation.
## Out
Completing the instance product, generations, task executor, fixing all existing loader assertions, real Telegram or LLM requests, production data.
## DONE WHEN
The local test/check command and hook/CI paths use isolation, preserve meaningful failures and bounded cleanup; hostile owner environment and interrupted test runs cannot modify the real checkout or leave their processes/resources alive. Docker mode uses its own daemon or fails explicitly if unsupported, never falls back to the owner daemon.

title: The loader initialises OpenBao, keeps unseal custody, unseals after every restart and retires the root token
description:
lifemodel-ryr stage 2. Using the phase machine: init OpenBao (Shamir 1-of-1 or 3-of-5 — choose and justify for a single-owner VM) once, write the unseal key(s) and root token to the custody Secret BEFORE using them, read back; unseal; create the loader's steady-state Bao role/policy needed later and RETIRE (revoke) the root token; on every loader start and on a watch/poll of seal status, unseal a sealed OpenBao. Network: loader -> openbao API only. Tests prove: one init, custody written before use, resume at each cut without re-init, unseal after a sealed restart, root token revoked and absent from the custody Secret afterwards.

title: lifemodel reaches the owner's model only through a platform-owned gateway that injects the key from OpenBao and fails over to the reserve
description:
Charter instance-1, outcomes 4 and 5. Split from lifemodel-2t5 by the owner (2026-10-16, "Разделить"): build now only what the target story needs — the chat answered by the owner's model with no key in lifemodel. Design: ADR-013 (`docs/adr/013-model-gateway.md`). A platform-owned `model-gateway` in `lifemodel-system`, built from the loader image, OpenAI-compatible `/v1` front for the core, keys read from OpenBao (`lifemodel/data/model/<slot>`, written by the loader's wizard, lifemodel-3wi9), key injected only upstream, failover to the reserve, `/status` health shown as "no connection to the model since …" in the chat and the loader.

title: The model gateway proxies the core's chat requests to the primary, injects the key from OpenBao and fails over to the reserve
description:
ADR-013 Decisions 2–5. In the loader package, a second entry point `model-gateway` (built into the same image, `node dist/model-gateway.js`): OpenAI-compatible `POST /v1/chat/completions` (SSE streaming passthrough) and `GET /v1/models`, `GET /status`; nothing else (404). Reads slots from OpenBao (`lifemodel/data/model/primary|reserve`, KV v2; a deleted latest version = unset) with its service-account login, 30 s cache, reread after upstream 401/403; drops any inbound Authorization; injects the slot key upstream only. Failover per ADR-013 D4 (connect 5 s, first byte 60 s; 5xx/429/connection/timeout/malformed → reserve; other 4xx returned; never mid-stream; reserve model id substituted; no reserve → 502 safe code). Destination validation reuses the loader's validator from lifemodel-3wi9.4.2 (same module). No key, upstream body or query URL in logs.
## DONE WHEN
Tests (fake Bao, local HTTP upstreams): every bullet of ADR-013 "Checks" gateway part, including an upstream that echoes the Authorization header never leaking it to the core or a recording logger; planted mutations (no failover on 5xx; failover mid-stream; inbound Authorization forwarded; reserve model not substituted) killed. Normally the full check is green.

The Bao client, cache and URL helper come from lifemodel-s9v5.1.4. Read ADR-013 whole.

title: The platform runs the model gateway under its own read-only OpenBao role, and the core reaches the model only through it
description:
ADR-013 Decisions 1, 3, 5, 7. Platform: Deployment/Service `model-gateway` in `lifemodel-system` in step A (after OpenBao), image = the loader image digest, its ServiceAccount and Kubernetes-auth role `model-gateway` with policy `read` on `lifemodel/data/model/*` only, provisioned in the loader's bootstrap policy action before root revocation (beside `loader-model`, idempotent, verified under the role before revocation). NetworkPolicies: gateway egress = the loader's model exception; gateway ingress from core pods on 8080 and from web/loader to `/status` port; the core's egress for the model only to the gateway. The core's settings point `baseUrl` at the gateway with no key (seeded by the platform/first start, no key field), and the platform no longer points the core at `llm-stub` (kept as a walk fixture).
## DONE WHEN
Tests: rendered manifests assert the Deployment, Service, RBAC, NetworkPolicies and image digest pin; the bootstrap phase's policy text and role binding asserted, and its ordering before revocation; the core's seeded settings contain the gateway URL and no key. Normally the full check is green.

NetworkPolicies both sides, two listeners 8080/8081, split lifemodel-system default-deny from the loader's allows, Bao ingress from the gateway [G-07]. Command override with the absolute path, own SA, no PVC/custody/PKI, read-only root, step-A digest pinned by the release flow with a release render test, readiness independent of slots [G-09].

title: The chat's Сейчас panel and the loader's settings show 'no connection to the model since HH:MM' from the gateway's status
description:
ADR-013 Decision 6. The web module reads the gateway's `/status` (server side, bounded, cached ≤ 10 s) and exposes it in its creature/state stream; the chat's "Сейчас" panel shows "Нет связи с моделью с HH:MM — <error in words>" / "No connection to the model since HH:MM — …" when the last attempt failed, nothing when OK. The loader's settings page shows the same line (it reads `/status` itself). Safe codes mapped to words in en/ru.
## DONE WHEN
Frontend tests: the panel and the loader settings render the line from a failing `/status` fixture and hide it on success, en/ru, both themes, axe-core clean; web module test: a `/status` timeout does not stall the state stream. Normally the full check is green.

title: A role-parameterised OpenBao client and slot reader serve both the loader and the model gateway, with renewal and typed storage errors
description:
ADR-013 Decision 3 [G-06] and Decision 2 URL helper [G-10]. A role-parameterised OpenBao client in the loader package (token in memory; projected JWT read afresh per login; renew/re-login before expiry; one bounded re-login on rejection; typed errors that never carry response bodies: sealed, unreachable, denied, not found), used by the loader (role `loader`) and the gateway (role `model-gateway`); the slot reader for KV v2 `lifemodel/data/model/<slot>` (deleted latest version = unset; storage errors never = unset) with the gateway's cache (30 s refresh, hard expiry after 5 min of failed refreshes → `storage_unavailable`, invalidation hook); the shared base-URL helper (complete API base, append `chat/completions`/`models`, keep prefix, normalise one trailing slash). The loader's existing Bao calls move onto this client without behaviour change.
## DONE WHEN
Tests with a fake Bao HTTP server: login, renewal, expiry, JWT rotation, rejection and one re-login, seal/unseal, denied, deleted vs missing vs unavailable; cache hard expiry and invalidation; URL helper table (`/v1`, `/v1/`, prefixed, bare host); no error message contains a response body (recording logger). Normally the full check is green.

comments.author: dev
comments.text: Carried from lifemodel-3wi9.4.2 (confirmation review T342-06, nonblocking): the loader's Bao model slots have no HTTP-boundary tests for a sealed (503) or denied (403) Bao behind GET /api/model, PUT /api/model/<slot> and DELETE /api/model/reserve, and none for the 403 → re-login with a freshly read projected service-account token path (loader/src/openbao.ts ~368-373). Generic storage exceptions already map to 503 storage_unavailable on all three routes. When this task moves the Bao access into the role-parameterised client, add those tests there (sealed, denied, unreachable → typed storage error → 503; token expiry → re-read token file → one retry).

title: Pods resolve names from the owner's LAN DNS: the platform hands k3s the host's usable nameservers
description:
Owner's combined test 2026-10-19: the owner's model https://llm.inside.shady2k.ru/v1 resolves on the VM host (LAN DNS 192.168.0.30 -> 192.168.0.137) but not in pods (ENOTFOUND), so the loader's model check answered {"error":"unreachable"}. Cause: the host /etc/resolv.conf lists 192.168.0.30 and an IPv6 link-local nameserver (fe80::...%ens18); k3s rejects it and falls back to 8.8.8.8 (/var/lib/rancher/k3s/agent/etc/resolv.conf). Worked around on the test VM only with a coredns-custom forward for inside.shady2k.ru.
Fix in the NixOS module and the generic-Linux installer: give k3s --resolv-conf a file with the host's usable nameservers (drop link-local/loopback; keep IPv4 and global IPv6), regenerated when the host's DNS changes; no per-domain rules.
DONE WHEN: render/unit tests for both install paths (link-local and loopback dropped, LAN nameserver kept, fallback only when none is usable); on the VM from a clean snapshot a LAN-only name resolves in a pod and the loader saves the owner's LAN model with no manual step; normally public names still resolve.

title: The owner opens the instance from outside under their own domain, with their own certificate or one issued by Let's Encrypt
description:
Idea (owner, 2026-10-08: 'Доступ снаружи позже сделаем'). In the loader, a section 'Access': the owner enters a domain; the loader lists the DNS records for boot., app., vault. and checks they point here; a certificate is either issued by Let's Encrypt (one SAN certificate for the three names via HTTP-01, auto-renewed - Caddy does this itself) or uploaded; 'listen beyond localhost' switches on only once HTTPS is ready, so the password never travels in clear. Builds on outcome 4's front door (Caddy, subdomains, local only, decision on lifemodel-q4x). Until then a user on a VPS reaches the instance through an SSH tunnel.

Observable criterion: with a domain pointing at the machine, the owner enters it in the loader and within minutes opens https://boot.<domain> from another device with a valid certificate; disproved if a manual certificate step or a plain-HTTP login is needed. Left out: dynamic DNS, several owners.

comments.author: claude-code
comments.text:
Owner decision 2026-10-16 — how the owner reaches the loader and the app (replaces the `*.localhost` + SSH tunnel used on the test VM):

- In the home network the instance is reached by an mDNS name the node announces itself (e.g. `http://lifemodel.local/`, loader at `boot.lifemodel.local`); the installer ends by printing that address. Plain HTTP, LAN only.
- First-start setup is open from the LAN without a one-time code or password ("так тоже часто делают"); once the password is set, login is required as today. Risk accepted by the owner: whoever on the LAN opens setup first sets the password.
- HTTPS is offered by binding the owner's own domain with a Let's Encrypt certificate (DNS-01, no inbound ports) — lifemodel-sd2. The wizard offers it; without it, access stays LAN-only HTTP and the PWA cannot be installed (secure context required).
- Tailscale is rejected: it is blocked for the owner. Because a domain allows wildcard names, the separate `boot.` host (origin isolation of the loader from the app) is kept.

comments.author: claude-code
comments.text:
Owner decision 2026-10-16 (amends the decision above: "HTTPS by default, as Proxmox does"):

- The installer creates the instance's own certificate authority and issues from it a server certificate for `lifemodel.local` and `boot.lifemodel.local`. The instance serves HTTPS from the first start; plain HTTP only redirects to HTTPS. LAN traffic, the setup wizard included, is never sent in clear.
- The installer ends by printing the address and the certificate's fingerprint, so the owner can check the browser's warning is for their own node.
- The loader offers the root certificate for download as an optional step. Installed on a device, it removes the warning and makes the PWA installable without a domain.
- Binding the owner's domain with Let's Encrypt (lifemodel-sd2) replaces this certificate; access from outside the LAN still needs the domain.

title: A panic command stops everything and nothing comes back until the owner resumes
description:
Charter: docs/charters/platform-1.md, outcome 3. Design: ADR-006 (loader commands, owner-controls).

## DONE WHEN
After a panic command to the loader and a reboot of the test VM no lifemodel process is running; a resume command brings it back.

title: A fresh install loses OpenBao's unseal key when sys/init outlasts the loader's 10-second client timeout
description:
**What happens.** On a fresh install the loader's first phase calls OpenBao `sys/init`. Its OpenBao client gives up after 10 s (`loader/src/model-bao.ts`, default `timeoutMs` 10_000). On a fresh single-node raft OpenBao, `sys/init` first waits for the raft election (heartbeat timeout 5 s). On the test VM on 2026-10-21 the init took 10.0 s (request 01:21:57.147, root token generated 01:22:07.177). The loader logged `unreachable` at 01:22:07.148, OpenBao finished initializing anyway, and the unseal key and root token were never received. Every retry since: "OpenBao is initialized but Secret openbao-unseal-custody is missing or invalid; restore its unseal key from recovery backup". The platform never comes up (A, B, C, D all not Ready); the only way out is wiping the instance.

**What should happen.** A fresh install never loses its init material because a response was slow: init is sent only once OpenBao can answer it within the client's bound (raft leader elected / `sys/health` reports initializable), or the init request's bound covers the first election, and the material reaches custody.

**Criterion.** A test with a fake OpenBao whose `sys/init` answers after the ordinary client timeout leads to custody being written, not to an initialized-without-custody instance; and a fresh VM install succeeds repeatedly. Disproved by any fresh install ending in the "initialized but … custody missing" state.

Pre-existing on main (not caused by lifemodel-653.7.8, whose walk met it; a repeat install passed the init). Related: lifemodel-p4xu, lifemodel-eoa8. Evidence kept from the walk: OpenBao and loader log excerpts (no secrets).
close_reason: accepted at 6eb0eee7: fixed in PR #108, fresh installs on the VM initialized OpenBao without loss through every stage-2 walk; stage-2 acceptance record on lifemodel-653.7

title: The machine and the cluster expose Prometheus metrics kept on the machine, and the agent reads its own footprint from them
description:
Owner, 2026-10-21: «Можно еще telegraf на vm ставить и отдавать prometheus метрики. Это будет полезно и
агенту, он сможет оценить свое влияние на машину и кластер.»

What: the machine and the cluster expose metrics in the Prometheus / OpenMetrics text format (the open
standard; any scraper and store can read it), collected on the machine and kept there.
- Machine: CPU, memory, disk and its free space, network, load — collected by an agent on the host,
  outside the cluster, so the numbers exist when k3s is down (owner's suggestion: Telegraf with its
  prometheus_client output; the Prometheus-native alternative is node_exporter; settle at charter). Like
  the supervisor (lifemodel-ahrm), not tied to NixOS: installed by the generic installer on any Linux.
- Cluster: per-module CPU/memory/restarts (kubelet/cAdvisor, kube-state-metrics or Telegraf's Kubernetes
  inputs) and the modules' own counters (model errors and latency per lifemodel-vbog).
- Storage of series on the machine with bounded retention (e.g. VictoriaMetrics beside VictoriaLogs of
  lifemodel-vbog); nothing leaves the machine.

For the agent (owner's reason): lifemodel reads its own footprint — what its turns, tasks and model calls
cost the machine and the cluster — through a narrow read-only port, never raw query access. This fits the
architecture's physiology: machine load is an interoceptive signal for the autonomic layer (energy, the
wake threshold), so the agent can, e.g., hold back a heavy task when the machine is under pressure.
Design of that port and its signals belongs to the charter, not here.

Feature title only until the milestone is chartered.

## DONE WHEN
On the test machine the owner opens one place and sees host and per-module CPU/memory/disk for the last
day, and the agent, asked what its last task cost the machine, answers from the metrics with numbers that
match them; it is falsified if the host numbers vanish while k3s is stopped.

comments.author: claude-code-coordinator
comments.text:
Owner, 2026-10-21: «vmagent например» — the collector/shipper: vmagent (VictoriaMetrics) scrapes Prometheus
endpoints (host exporter, kubelet/cAdvisor, modules) and remote-writes to VictoriaMetrics, buffering on its
own disk while the store is unavailable. Fits the VictoriaLogs choice of lifemodel-vbog (one vendor stack,
Prometheus/OpenMetrics in, PromQL/MetricsQL out). Host numbers still come from an agent on the host
(node_exporter or Telegraf), which vmagent scrapes; vmagent itself can run on the host beside the
supervisor so collection survives k3s being down.

title: Modules authenticate each other with mTLS workload identities once they span machines or come from foreign sources
description:
Deferred by the owner, 2026-10-12 (ADR-010 simplification points 0 and 3, comments on lifemodel-b0r.9). Today isolation is structural: Docker networks (internal modules network, egress/vault/docker/front-* networks), per-module Valkey/Postgres roles, the egress gateway knows a requester by the stream it wrote to. Module code is trusted against malice, not bugs.

Return when: modules run on several machines, or a module comes from a foreign source (third-party plugin). Then: loader-minted SPIFFE-like identities (spiffe://<trust-domain>/<instance>/<generation>/<module>), every peer surface verifies the identity, policy derived from it.

Criterion: a module presenting another module's name without its identity is refused at every surface; disproved by a spoofed call that succeeds.
Left out: certificate rotation UI, external CA.

comments.author: dev
comments.text: Owner, 2026-10-13: on k3s, mTLS between modules comes from a service mesh - Istio (ambient mode: ztunnel per node, no sidecars, L4 mTLS + identity-based AuthorizationPolicy) or Linkerd as the lighter alternative. No own certificate issuance. Still deferred; return conditions unchanged.

title: Long work such as the news digest runs as a background task, so the conversation is never blocked by it
description:
Idea (owner, 2026-10-07). Today the news digest is done inside a cognition turn: the schedule news_digest_morning/evening_default (src/plugins/news/index.ts:764-911, handleDailyDigest) wakes cognition, which reads articles and composes the digest while holding the single cognition slot (pendingCognition); only Motor Cortex runs in the background. A message the owner sends meanwhile waits for the digest to end.

Ouroboros (docs/architecture/06-agent-core.md) separates short direct turns (owner chat, wakes) from durable queued tasks with their own lifecycle and stored results.

Proposal: a cognition turn stays short (decide, answer or delegate); long work becomes a task, a generalized Motor Cortex: durable record, recovery after restart (recoverOnRestart exists), result returned as a signal that a short turn delivers. The digest becomes such a task.

Observable criterion: while a digest is being prepared, a message from the owner is answered within the time of an ordinary turn, and the digest still arrives. Disproved if the answer waits for the digest.

Relations: may retire most of lifemodel-aeg (dialogue-1, a message taken into account at every boundary of a proactive turn); a self-change (lifemodel-n6r) also fits as a task.

Left out: choosing the task runner (internal pipeline vs prime-agent), task priorities, cancellation.

Added 2026-10-08 (owner: 'это должны быть задания'): reminders (one-shot and recurring schedule firings) and Motor Cortex results are tasks too. Today a firing is marked done before its signal is processed and a queued signal is lost on a restart or when another turn is busy or the aggregation picks another signal; a completed Motor Cortex result can be lost the same way (pre-existing on main; an acknowledge-after-processing attempt in lifemodel-ctc was rolled back because the core does not know which signals a turn consumed). As tasks they get a durable record and an outcome, so nothing depends on a signal surviving the in-memory queue. Observable criterion added: a reminder due while a turn is busy, or across a restart, is still delivered once.

title: A coordinator's run time is attributed to phases, so a run's summary compares work with its forecast
description:
Close-out retrospective of lifemodel-vhd and lifemodel-3wi9 (2026-10-19). Both runs came in under forecast on every forecast phase (vhd: build 48 of 300 min; 3wi9: build 189 of 540), but most of the occupied time is 'unattributed': vhd 46 of 94 min, 3wi9 277 of 474 min (coordinator design, reviews, VM walks, tracker work). Cause as the record holds it: the coordinator's long session spans several features and its work carries no phase marks, so the summary cannot say where the time went. Finding budget of instance-1 is spent (10/10) -> deferred; owner decides whether it enters a milestone.
Wanted: the coordinator's own work in a run is attributed to plan/build/debug/wrap (or a coordinator phase) so the forecast comparison means something.

title: Long work runs as a chain of tasks that continue from the previous branch and notes, with a build cache keyed by image and lockfile
description:
Owner, 2026-10-21: «И кэш, если задача длительная и нам нужно работать с ней постоянно?» — agreed («Да»)
to the direction below.

A single forever-running task does not fit the runtime: each task has a hard stop, exactly one harness
execution, and its working volume is removed when it ends (lifemodel-653 DONE WHEN). Long or continuous
work is therefore a **chain of tasks with continuity**: each next task starts from the previous one's
branch (the same git bundle path as the git-repository feature) and its state notes, which the
previous task marked as an artifact; progress lives in git and the storage module, not in a live
container, so it survives restarts and workbench updates.

Caches: toolchain and lifemodel's dev dependencies are baked into the workbench image (decided). A
project's build cache (its node_modules, incremental compiler output) is keyed by workbench digest +
lockfile hash and offered read-only to the next task of the same project (a shared read-only volume or
a storage artifact pulled at start); a miss only costs time, never correctness.

Questions to settle when picked up: who decides the next link (the agent, a schedule, the owner); how
the chain is shown to the owner as one piece of work; cache size bounds and eviction (counts toward the
20 GB ledger or its own).

Not in motor-1. Feature title only until planned.

## DONE WHEN
On the test VM a piece of work that needs three tasks in a row finishes with each task continuing from
the previous one's branch and notes, the second and third tasks start with a warm build cache (measured
start time lower than a cold one), and the owner sees one piece of work with three steps.

title: The owner sees what every part of the platform did: logs of all modules collected on the machine and searched in the loader's interface
description:
Owner decision 2026-10-19: 'В следующую. Причем давай сделаем следующей вехой именно наблюдаемость' — observability is the milestone right after motor-1, before generations-1.

Why: diagnosing a gateway bad_response on the test VM (lifemodel-mx6r) needed an in-pod probe: the gateway logs only an error code, logs live only in each pod's stdout (kubectl logs, lost on restart), and there are no metrics or a request id across chat, core and gateway.

Agreed direction (to be chartered through to-milestone): logs of every platform module collected and kept on the machine across restarts (e.g. VictoriaLogs or Loki with Vector; nothing leaves the machine, logs hold personal data); a logs page in the loader's interface behind its login, with search and filters by time, module, level and conversation id (owner: 'веб-интерфейс нужно будет добавить логи'; the loader works when the core or chat is broken); safe structured failure reasons (field and type, never values); basic metrics (model errors, latency, restarts); one request id from the chat through the core to the gateway.

Feature title only until the milestone is chartered.

## DONE WHEN
On the test VM, after a planted model failure and a restart of the failing module, the owner opens the loader's logs page, finds the failure by time and conversation id, and reads which module failed and why (field and type, no values); it is falsified if any step needs kubectl or a probe.

title: Core ticks and cognition turns are recorded as traces in the observability database
description:
Core ticks and cognition turns write span trees (tick → layers → LLM calls → tools → intents) into the `observability` Postgres schema introduced for task runs by lifemodel-653.8.24, so "why did the agent do that" is answered from the database by `lifemodel doctor trace`, not from pod stdout. Model: hermes-lifemodel's SpanLogger (no log without a span; durable-first, then the human log line) and turn recorder. Fail-open, bounded, retention as in 653.8.24.
Left out: log shipping of other modules (lifemodel-vbog), metrics (lifemodel-sw1s).
Disproved if a cognition turn's tool calls and LLM requests cannot be read back as one tree by trace id.

title: The owner talks to lifemodel through the web interface
description:
Charter: docs/charters/instance-1.md, outcome 8 (new 2026-10-11, owner; lifemodel-he0). The channel of this milestone: the owner talks to lifemodel in a web chat served behind the loader's front door and the owner's password, on the container shape of outcome 5 - messages enter the Valkey event bus and lifemodel's answers come back from it, so a switch of generations does not break the conversation. Telegram is out of this milestone and returns later on the same shape.

Behind the loader's password the owner writes in the web chat and gets lifemodel's answer, and the conversation survives a switch of generations: no message lost or answered twice.

title: The core and the storage seam serve a web module: idempotent intake, the web recipient, the creature state, replies and a cursor-safe transcript
description:
Stage 1 of lifemodel-vhd. ADR-011 Decisions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and D3: what the core and the storage seam must give a web module before it exists. All behind the D4 operations in `src/storage/` and `src/ports/` (`acceptOwnerMessage`, `readTranscript`, `watchTranscript`, `readCreatureState`); the core stays the only writer of `core.conversation_messages`. Out: the HTTP server (stage 2), the app (stage 3), the cluster (stage 4).

## DONE WHEN
Suite tests against the launcher's Valkey and Postgres show: an owner message accepted through `acceptOwnerMessage` becomes one logical input across crash, concurrent and late retries, a conflicting retry and a stale id are refused (S1); the core writes first to the owner's web recipient with no message before, and keeps the same recipient after a restart (S12); the creature state is published with freshness and replaced at once by a restarted core (S11, core side); a reply's quoted message reaches the turn's context and the owner row (S13, core side); `readTranscript` returns only visible rows by a recipient cursor that never skips a row under overlapping saves, and one page of 10,000 rows (S4 ordering, S9 query).

title: The core makes the owner's web recipient its primary recipient at start and writes first to it, with no Telegram conversion
description:
ADR-011 Decision 4 (VHD-04). The owner's web recipient has channel `web` and destination `owner`, so its id is deterministic in the recipient registry. At start the core durably upserts it and makes it the primary recipient; this replaces the Telegram chat-id conversion (`src/core/container.ts` sets the Telegram chat id to null; `src/core/core-loop.ts` establishes primary routing only through it and hardcodes `telegram`; `src/layers/aggregation/threshold-engine.ts` suppresses proactive contact without a primary recipient). Aggregation, the autonomic filters and every other primary-recipient consumer get it directly. The outbound trim floor is the Postgres apply offset alone.

## DONE WHEN
A suite test triggers proactive contact with no owner message before and finds an assistant row for the web recipient (`web`/`owner`); after a core restart the same recipient id and transcript are used (S12); no code path converts a Telegram chat id into the primary recipient (`grep -rn "telegram" src/core src/layers/aggregation` shows no primary-recipient routing); normally a user_message from the web recipient is answered to the same recipient.
close_reason: accepted with stage lifemodel-vhd.3 (acceptance record on the stage); on main via PR #45 (7b8dda3) and PR #46 (c4f1e0a); acceptance walk on lifemodel-vhd.1

title: The core publishes the creature state with freshness, and a stale or absent state reads as no state
description:
ADR-011 D3 (VHD-05 freshness). The core publishes `{ state, epoch, publishedAt }` (`thinking`, `awake`, `asleep`) to one Valkey key with a 15 s expiry: on every change, every 5 s as a heartbeat, and right after it takes the epoch at start. Not part of the commit. `readCreatureState()` returns the state and its age, and reports "no state" when the key is absent or older than 15 s.

## DONE WHEN
A suite test sees `thinking` while a turn runs and `awake` after it; with the core stopped after it published `thinking`, `readCreatureState()` reports no fresh state within 15 s; a restarted core replaces the stale state on start, before its first tick (S11, core side); normally the heartbeat keeps the key's age under 6 s.

title: An owner message is accepted once through a Valkey intake script with 7-day receipts and a server-side id age check
description:
ADR-011 Decisions 1 and 2 (VHD-01, VHD-02). `acceptOwnerMessage(id, text, replyTo?)` builds the full `user_message` signal (`signal.id = data.updateId = id`, `data.channel = 'web'`, the web recipient of lifemodel-vhd.3.1) and runs one Valkey script: with no receipt `inbound:receipt:<id>` it XADDs the `inbound.message` entry (`messageId = id`) first and then sets the receipt `{ streamId, sha256(text) }` with a 7-day expiry; same hash returns the original `streamId`; different hash returns `conflict` and appends nothing. Before the script, the UUIDv7 time is checked: older than 24 h or more than 5 min ahead is `stale`. Inputs are validated before the call. A receipt-write failure after the append is an error; its retry appends a second entry with the same `messageId`, which the core's dedup absorbs. The core's owner row key stays `inbound:<id>`.

## DONE WHEN
A suite test against real Valkey and the core shows one logical input and the original `streamId` for: a retry after a crash between the append and the response; concurrent retries from two callers before the core reads; a retry after 1,001 later messages; and returns `conflict` for the same id with different text, `stale` for an id older than 24 h and for one more than 5 min ahead, and an error on an injected receipt-write failure whose retry is still one input (S1); normally a fresh id is accepted and answered once.
close_reason: accepted with stage lifemodel-vhd.3 (acceptance record on the stage); on main via PR #45 (7b8dda3) and PR #46 (c4f1e0a); acceptance walk on lifemodel-vhd.1

title: The owner-visible transcript is read and watched by a recipient cursor that never skips or repeats a row
description:
ADR-011 Decision 5 and D2 (VHD-07, VHD-08). `readTranscript({ before | after, limit ≤ 50 })` is a direct recipient-scoped keyset query over `core.conversation_messages`, never the core's whole-history load. Visible rows: `kind = 'message'` with role `user`, or role `assistant` with text content and no tool calls; tool rows, statuses, actions and compaction summaries are never returned, and clear markers or compaction do not hide history. DTO `{ sequence (decimal string), clientId?, role, text, createdAt, replyTo? }`; the latest page's `cursor` is the recipient's newest visible `sequence`, read in the same query. `watchTranscript(after)` yields rows after a cursor, woken by an XREAD BLOCK on `outbound` as a hint with a 1 s fallback poll. Invalid cursor is an error; a cursor ahead of the newest row gives an empty result.

## DONE WHEN
Suite tests show: with overlapping saves on separate connections, a delayed transaction, a rollback and a conflict retry, `watchTranscript` never skips or repeats a row (S4 ordering); with wake hints dropped the fallback poll alone delivers every row; over 10,000 rows the first page is ≤ 50 visible rows and earlier pages come by cursor with no internal rows (S9 query); normally a new assistant row reaches a watcher within 2 s.
close_reason: accepted with stage lifemodel-vhd.3 (acceptance record on the stage); on main via PR #45 (7b8dda3) and PR #46 (c4f1e0a); acceptance walk on lifemodel-vhd.1

title: A reply to an earlier message reaches the turn's context and is stored on the owner's row
description:
ADR-011 Decision 1, replies (S13). A `user_message` signal may carry `data.replyTo = { sequence, role, excerpt ≤ 280 chars }`, set by the intake after checking the row exists and is visible (lifemodel-vhd.3.3 validates; this task consumes it). The core adds the quoted message to the turn's context, and stores `replyTo` in the owner row's payload so `readTranscript` returns it.

## DONE WHEN
A suite test sends a reply to an earlier visible row and finds the quoted message in the turn's built context and `replyTo` on the owner row and its transcript DTO; a reply to an unknown or invisible sequence is refused by `acceptOwnerMessage` and appends nothing; normally a message without `replyTo` builds the same context as before.

title: The web module's server accepts messages, serves the transcript and streams new rows and the creature state
description:
Stage 2 of lifemodel-vhd. ADR-011 Decisions 3 and 6: the web module's server in `src/web/` — Fastify on Node 24, hand-written SSE, bundled by esbuild into one file — over the stage 1 operations only, never a raw store client. Out: the React app (stage 3), the image, routes and Deployment (stage 4).

## DONE WHEN
Suite tests drive the server over HTTP against the launcher's stores and a running core: `POST /api/messages` gives 202 once per logical input and 409/403/400/503 for conflict, stale, bad Origin, bad body and receipt failure (S1 over HTTP, S6); `GET /api/transcript` and `GET /api/events` deliver every visible row once across a row inserted between page read and subscription, repeated drops mid-batch, `Last-Event-ID` resume, state-only intervals and duplicate delivery (S4); with the server stopped while the core commits, a restart's catch-up shows each row once (S8); the state event turns stale within 15 s of a core kill (S11 stream); every response carries the CSP and `no-store` headers (S7 header); `npm run build` produces the one-file server bundle.

title: The web module accepts owner messages over POST /api/messages behind an exact Origin check
description:
ADR-011 Decision 3, HTTP surface and security rules. `src/web/` server skeleton (Fastify, request schemas, esbuild one-file bundle wired into `npm run build`) with `POST /api/messages`: body `{ id, text, replyTo? }` — UUIDv7 `id`, non-empty text ≤ 16 KiB, `replyTo` a decimal sequence string; the server derives recipient and channel. The Origin must parse to exactly `http://localhost` (missing, `null`, malformed, sibling host, other scheme or port → 403; no CORS). Calls `acceptOwnerMessage`: accepted or duplicate → 202 with `{ streamId }`; conflict or stale → 409 with the reason; receipt failure → 503. Body size and send-rate limits. Logs carry request id, client id and intake result, never text, cookies or credentials.

## DONE WHEN
Unit tests on the Origin guard and body validation cover each refused case and the accepted one (S6); an integration test over HTTP repeats lifemodel-vhd.3.3's S1 cases through the route and gets 202/409/503 as specified with one logical input each; a log-capture test finds no message text in the server's logs; normally a valid send returns 202 and the core answers it.

title: The web module serves the transcript and an SSE stream that delivers every visible row once and the creature state
description:
ADR-011 Decisions 5 and 6. `GET /api/transcript?before=<seq>&limit=50` returns the projection newest first with `cursor`; `GET /api/events?after=<cursor>` is SSE: catch-up in order in batches of ≤ 50 with the row `sequence` as the SSE id, then live rows from `watchTranscript`; `state` events carry no id and the current state goes first on every subscription; `Last-Event-ID` resumes; heartbeat comment every 15 s; flush per event; a bounded per-stream queue that closes the stream past its bound; ≤ 4 concurrent streams per session; streams close after 15 minutes. `Cache-Control: no-store` on private responses.

## DONE WHEN
Integration tests show every visible row rendered once by a test client across: a row inserted between the page read and the subscription, repeated drops in the middle of a batch, a new EventSource after a reload, state-only intervals, duplicate delivery and dropped wake hints (S4); with the server stopped while the core commits rows, its restart's catch-up shows each once (S8); a core killed after `thinking` turns the stream's state stale within 15 s (S11); normally a new answer reaches an open stream within 2 s.

title: The chat page renders: the web server's transcript response matches the web app's TranscriptPage contract
description:
The chat page stays blank in a real browser: the web app throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')` on its first transcript load.

What happens (VM walk 2026-10-17, Chromium 1243, web image sha256:4f333224…, loader 5e1ef49): after login and handoff, `https://lifemodel.local/` loads the app, `/api/transcript?limit=50` answers 200 with `{rows: [], cursor: null}`, the app reads `page.messages.length` and crashes; the body is empty. The same blank page is in the 4.1 walk screenshot, so it predates the loader work.

Cause: contract mismatch on main. `src/web/server.ts` returns the `TranscriptReader` result (`src/ports/transcript.ts`: `{ rows: TranscriptRow[], cursor: string | null }`), while `web/app/src/transport.ts` expects `TranscriptPage { messages: TranscriptMessage[]; cursor: string }` (and `TranscriptMessage` field names). Each side is tested against its own double, so no test crosses the boundary.

What should happen: the chat renders an empty conversation (and later rows) — ADR-011's web API contract decides the shape; the server and the app agree on it, `cursor: null` on an empty transcript is handled, and the SSE `message` events use the same message shape.

## DONE WHEN
A contract test exercises the real web server's `/api/transcript` (and one SSE `message` event) and parses the response with the app's own transport types/parsers (shared types or a shared schema), failing on today's mismatch; an empty transcript (`cursor: null`) and a non-empty one render in the app test. Normally the full check is green; the coordinator walks the chat on the VM.

title: lifemodel installs into an existing cluster inside its own namespace, with each platform dependency switchable to an external one
description:
Owner, 2026-10-13: lifemodel can be installed into an existing Kubernetes cluster the owner already runs, without Flux and without touching the cluster beyond lifemodel's own namespace and its operator ("ломать мой кластер я бы не дал"). The approach is the usual one of other projects' Helm charts: each platform dependency has a toggle, and disabling it requires an external one (e.g. `openbao.enabled=false` requires the address and auth of an external OpenBao; the same for Postgres, the registry, ingress). The operator applies the platform inside its namespace itself. Cluster-scoped pieces of the VM shape (Flux, CNPG's CRDs, the Bank-Vaults mutating webhook, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Traefik) are absent or optional here and the design names what replaces each. Deferred from instance-1, which delivers only a dedicated VM (ADR-010).

Left out: the dedicated-VM path (instance-1).

## DONE WHEN
In a test cluster that already runs other workloads, one helm install puts lifemodel into its own namespace with OpenBao, Postgres and the registry switched to external ones; nothing cluster-scoped is created; generations, rollback and panic work as on the VM.

title: The owner backs up the whole instance off the machine and restores it onto a clean one
description:
Owner, 2026-10-21 (with the supervisor outside the cluster, «давай так и сделаем»): the real insurance when a
machine cannot be repaired is a copy of the whole instance off the machine and a proven restore onto a
clean one.

Today nothing backs up the instance as a whole. lifemodel-653.7.4 restores only the task storage
(SeaweedFS + its catalog). Not covered: the Postgres database (conversations, memory, soul, settings),
Valkey state, Gitea (the repository and deploy branch), OpenBao and its unseal custody, the loader's own
volume (platform settings, CA, auth).

Questions to settle when picked up: where copies go (another disk, NAS, cloud — nothing leaves the
machine unless the owner chooses it; copies hold personal data and secrets, so they are encrypted); how
often and how many are kept; restore driven by the supervisor (lifemodel-* supervisor feature) onto a
clean machine; consistency across stores (one point in time or per store with a stated gap); the measured
restore time and backup age.

Feature title only; not in motor-1.

## DONE WHEN
On a clean test machine, the owner restores the instance from a backup with one command and finds the
conversation, memory, settings and task output as they were at the backup time; it is falsified if any
store is missing or a step needs manual SQL, kubectl or copying keys by hand.
